strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and important problem: scalable, architecture-agnostic uncertainty quantification for MLIPs, where Deep Ensembles are accurate but prohibitively expensive for large pretrained models.

The method is clearly presented: the variational formulation (Sec. 3), the adaptive variational dropout parameterization with input-dependent coefficients, and the local reparameterization trick (Alg. 1) are all well-motivated and technically correct, with closed-form KL derivations in the appendix.

The evaluation spans three complementary regimes: an illustrative dynamical system, data-scarce/OOD ammonia training from scratch, and fine-tuning a large pretrained model (ORB v3, 699-atom silica). Experiments follow established protocols (Tan et al. 2023) and are averaged over multiple seeds.

Results are generally convincing: BLIP outperforms MC Dropout baselines in NLL/CRPS/ECE across settings, and MAP inference gives a single-model, ensemble-competitive accuracy at deterministic-model cost.

The paper is honest about limitations: Section 3.3 explicitly acknowledges the invariance restriction of the current formulation excludes important equivariant MLIPs (MACE, UMA), and the silica results openly report that Deep Ensemble achieves a better Spearman correlation.
Reproducibility is reasonably supported: code release, public datasets, shared hyperparameters (Table 4), and detailed architectures/training procedures in the appendix.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core contribution is an application of adaptive Variational Dropout (Kingma et al. 2015; Coscia et al. 2025) to the message/update functions of MPNNs. The conceptual machinery is imported rather than new; the main novelty is domain-specific integration.

Evaluation scope is narrow relative to the claims: no standard MLIP benchmarks (MD17, MD22, SPICE, OC20/MPtrj, etc.) are used. The claim of scalability to 'large-scale foundation models' rests on a single fine-tuning experiment on one material (SiO2), which does not substantiate scalability claims.

The claimed accuracy improvement is fragile: gains are clearest in extremely small-data regimes (78 ammonia samples; 32-128 silica samples) where the KL-regularized stochastic weights likely act as a regularizer. At 1024 silica samples (Fig. 3b), BLIP vs. non-BLIP differences appear within standard error. The paper does not disentangle UQ benefits from regularization effects.

Baseline reporting is incomplete: Deep Ensemble NLL/CRPS in Table 1 are marked 'NA', so the headline claim that BLIP is 'best-calibrated' in the non-equivariant setting cannot be fully verified against the strongest competitor. Deep Ensemble also outperforms BLIP on Spearman correlation (0.676 vs 0.602) in the silica experiment, which is the metric most relevant to the motivating active-learning use case.
No active learning experiment is performed despite the framing of UQ's value for active learning pipelines; the Spearman correlation analysis is a proxy rather than a demonstration.

Hyperparameter fragility: the KL weight λ varies by three orders of magnitude across experiments (0.01, 10, 0.001), and the ORB v3 setup requires aggressive clamping of dropout probabilities and reduced priors because the pretrained model is 'highly sensitive' to perturbations. This suggests the method may be difficult to apply robustly in practice, undermining the 'drop-in tool' claim.

The equivariance limitation is significant in 2026: the most competitive modern MLIP architectures (MACE, UMA, and other irreps-based models) are explicitly excluded, restricting practical reach to invariant MPNNs or older equivariant models like PaiNN.

Inference-time cost of calibrated UQ (100 stochastic forward passes in Sec. 4.3) is not compared quantitatively with ensemble cost under matched compute, so efficiency claims would benefit from more careful accounting.

strengths: The paper addresses a real and timely problem: principled, scalable uncertainty quantification (UQ) for machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs), where Deep Ensembles are currently the de facto standard but are expensive.

The method is clearly described: adaptive Variational Dropout applied to message and update functions, with input-dependent coefficients from a shared invariant inference network, closed-form KL terms (Appendix A.1), and practical algorithms (local reparameterization, training and inference pseudocode) that would allow reimplementation.

The evaluation covers three regimes (training from scratch on a toy N-body system, data-scarce/OOD training on ammonia, and fine-tuning a large pretrained model on silica glass), and reports both predictive accuracy (MAE/MSE) and calibration metrics (NLL, CRPS, ECE, Spearman correlation), which is more thorough than many UQ papers.

Results are positive on the chosen benchmarks: BLIP beats MC Dropout and roughly matches or exceeds 4-member Deep Ensembles at lower cost, and fine-tuning with BLIP outperforms deterministic fine-tuning and the pretrained PaiNN ensemble baseline.

Reproducibility support is reasonably good: datasets are public, splits follow prior work, hyperparameters (Table 4, Appendix C) and implementation details are provided, and code availability is stated.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core contribution is Variational Dropout (Kingma et al., 2015) with input-dependent adaptive coefficients, explicitly following Coscia et al. (2025), applied to MPNNs. The conceptual step from BARNN-style adaptive variational dropout to graph message passing is incremental rather than a new inference framework.

The equivariance treatment is a significant theoretical gap for this application area. Section 3.3 concedes that the method in its current form is incompatible with irreducible-representation networks, which excludes most leading modern MLIPs (MACE, UMA, Allegro-class models) that the paper itself cites as state of the art. Individual stochastic passes also break equivariance (footnote 3), which is problematic for force predictions in molecular dynamics.

The empirical evidence is narrow relative to the paper's broad claims of being a 'scalable, architecture-agnostic' framework. Experiments use only a 5-particle toy system, a single small molecule (NH3, 78 training points), and one fine-tuning task (SiO2) on one architecture (ORB v3). No standard MLIP benchmarks (MD17/MD22, OC20/OC22 subset, MATPES-style evaluations) and no ablation over architectures are provided.

Some headline claims are not fully supported. 'Minimal computational overhead' and 'no additional computational cost' for UQ conflict with the inference protocol requiring 100 stochastic forward passes (sample-mean) per structure; only the MAP estimate is single-pass, and its accuracy advantage over the deterministic baseline is not consistently established. The Spearman correlation result on silica (0.602 vs 0.676 for Deep Ensemble) is reported almost in passing despite being the metric most relevant to the motivating active-learning use case, and no actual active learning experiment is run despite active learning motivating the entire introduction.

Statistical robustness of the gains is questionable: the ammonia force MAE improvement (41.93 ± 3.38 vs 48.03 for Deep Ensemble) has large error bars, the equivariant N-body setting shows Deep Ensembles actually beat BLIP on MSE, NLL, and CRPS, and in the 1024-sample silica regime all fine-tuning variants converge to nearly identical MAE, so the advantage is confined to the very-low-data regime.

The KL weighting λ varies by three orders of magnitude across experiments (0.001 to 10) with different prior dropout probabilities (0.5 vs 0.01) and clamping heuristics per task, suggesting the method is sensitive to tuning and that reported results may depend on per-benchmark hyperparameter search whose protocol is not described. The paper also lacks an explicit limitations section discussing these sensitivities, the energy-head-only results on silica (forces are shown in Fig. 3b but energy MAE is not reported), and the ensemble size sensitivity of the Deep Ensemble baselines (4 members is small by literature standards).

strengths: Addresses a practically important and well-motivated problem: principled, scalable uncertainty quantification for MLIPs, where deep ensembles are costly and single-model UQ methods underperform (Tan et al., 2023 is cited and directly built upon).

The method is architecture-agnostic and integrates cleanly with existing MPNNs via adaptive variational dropout with the local reparameterization trick, keeping inference cost at the level of a deterministic model when uncertainty is not needed (Algorithm 4).

Honest and clear discussion of the equivariance limitation (Section 3.3): the current formulation requires an invariant inference network and excludes models with irreducible-representation layers such as MACE and UMA; the paper correctly identifies this as an open gap rather than overclaiming.

Experiments span three regimes (toy N-body, data-scarce/OOD ammonia, fine-tuning a large pretrained ORB v3 model on silica glass with 699-atom structures), and include prediction accuracy, calibration (ECE), and error-uncertainty correlation (Spearman), which is the right set of metrics for the active-learning motivation.

Reproducibility is reasonably strong: datasets are public with the same splits as prior work, hyperparameters and architectures are detailed in Appendix C, algorithms are given in pseudocode, KL derivations are in Appendix A, and code is stated to be released.

Results on ammonia show both better force MAE (41.93 vs 48.03 for deep ensembles) and better ECE (0.091 vs 0.108), and fine-tuning with BLIP outperforms deterministic fine-tuning and the PaiNN ensemble baseline at lower cost.
weaknesses: Limited originality: the core method is an input-dependent (adaptive) variant of variational dropout (Kingma et al., 2015), with the adaptive parameterization explicitly credited to Coscia et al. (2025). The contribution is largely an application/adaptation of known machinery to MPNN-based MLIPs rather than a new inference technique; the theoretical analysis (Section 3.3) is brief.

Empirical breadth is thin for the claims made: only two chemistry benchmarks beyond the toy system, a single base architecture per task, and deep ensembles limited to 4 members. Several baseline entries are NA (no std, no NLL/CRPS for deep ensembles in Table 1), which weakens the comparison against the strongest UQ competitor.

Improvements on some targets are marginal: ammonia energy MAE 11.51 +/- 0.75 vs 11.71 for deep ensembles is within noise; in the equivariant N-body setting deep ensembles still beat BLIP on all three metrics. Claims of 'improved predictive accuracy with respect to standard MLIPs' should be tempered.

Sensitivity to key hyperparameters is not analyzed: the KL weight lambda varies by three orders of magnitude across experiments (0.01, 10, 0.001), prior dropout p differs across tasks, and the silica experiments require heavy clamping (p in [1e-5, 0.1]) because ORB v3 is 'highly sensitive to even minimal perturbations'. No ablation over lambda, p, number of MC samples, or the benefit of adaptive vs. fixed coefficients is provided.

The paper motivates active learning repeatedly but never runs an active learning experiment; only a Spearman correlation between predicted variance and squared error is reported, and on silica BLIP underperforms deep ensembles on this metric (0.602 vs 0.676).

Per-sample weight noise technically breaks equivariance of individual forward passes (acknowledged only in a footnote); the implications for force prediction symmetry and for MD stability are not empirically examined.

The variational posterior is conditioned only on the initial node features and edge attributes and shared across all layers, which is efficient but a coarse approximation; no discussion or experiment probes how this restriction affects uncertainty quality.
No limitations section in the main text; the equivariance gap and hyperparameter sensitivity issues are scattered through the paper rather than consolidated.

strengths: The core method (input-dependent variational dropout with local reparameterization applied to MPNN message/update functions) is practical, scalable, and genuinely architecture-agnostic within its applicable class; it requires only a single model and adds minimal parameter overhead (Table 6 shows ×1.001 parameters, ×1.9 training FLOPs, no inference overhead).

Comprehensive and well-chosen experimental suite spanning an illustrative N-body system, a data-scarce/OOD ammonia task with published baselines (Tan et al., 2023), fine-tuning a large pretrained foundation model (ORB v3) on silica glass across data sizes, and an active-learning pipeline on MATPES — covering both 'train from scratch' and 'fine-tune' settings, which strengthens the practical significance.

Results support the main claims in several settings: BLIP beats all published baselines on ammonia MAE (11.51/41.93) with best ECE (0.091); in the AL experiment, uncertainty-guided selection clearly outperforms random selection within BLIP, isolating the value of the UQ signal.

The equivariance treatment is unusually careful for this line of work: a formal proposition on stochastic equivariant maps (Appendix A.3) with an honest analysis that local reparameterization breaks equivariance for irrep-based models, and this limitation is stated rather than hidden.

Useful computational cost analysis (Appendix E) quantifying the trade-off against deep ensembles, and reasonably complete hyperparameter/implementation details in the appendix supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the approach is a direct adaptation of Variational Dropout (Kingma et al., 2015) with input-dependent coefficients following Coscia et al. (2025) (BARNN), applied to MPNN layers. The conceptual contribution is incremental — the paper's value rests mostly on the empirical transfer to the MLIP setting.

The 'seamlessly integrates with a vast family of invariant and equivariant models' claim is overstated: by the authors' own analysis (Sec. 3.3, Appendix A.3), local reparameterization breaks equivariance for irrep-based architectures, excluding MACE and UMA — arguably the most important modern equivariant MLIPs. The demonstrated architectures (PaiNN, EGNN, ORB v3) are precisely those that avoid this issue, so generality within equivariant MLIPs remains unproven.

Mixed UQ evidence weakens the 'trustworthy/calibrated uncertainty' narrative: BLIP's Spearman correlation is worse than Gaussian Mixture Model on ammonia (0.863 vs 0.904) and worse than Deep Ensemble on silica (0.602 vs 0.676); the silica ECE advantage (0.032 vs 0.247) is striking but unexplained and may reflect a degenerate variance scale given the heavily clamped VAD coefficients [1e-5, 0.11].

Signs of hyperparameter fragility: the KL weight λ varies by four orders of magnitude across experiments (0.001 to 10), coefficient clamping is required 'for stability', and pretrained ORB weights are described as 'highly sensitive to even minimal perturbations'. No sensitivity analysis or ablation over λ/clamping is provided.

Baseline gaps: single-model UQ baselines (MC Dropout, evidential, mean-variance) from Tan et al. (2023) are compared on ammonia but not re-run on the silica/MATPES fine-tuning experiments; the active-learning experiment lacks a 'w/o BLIP' arm with any uncertainty-free selection comparison beyond random-within-BLIP, and Table 4 reports only 3 seeds; Table 1's Deep Ensemble entries have ±NA uncertainties, which is unexplained and confusing.

No molecular dynamics validation (trajectory stability, drift) despite MLIPs' primary use case being simulation; energy conservation for the stochastic potential (forces as gradients of a stochastically perturbed energy) is not discussed in the UQ setting.

Presentation quality is below the bar in places: typos ('data-scarse', 'memebers', 'Finetuing', 'deepensembling', 'the once induced'), and reproducibility would be strengthened by an explicit code-release statement.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely important problem: scalable, single-model uncertainty quantification for MLIPs, which is central to active learning and safe simulations.

The method is well-motivated and practical: adaptive variational dropout with a lightweight amortized inference network and local reparameterization keeps memory overhead near zero (Table 6) and inference cost identical to the deterministic backbone in MAP mode.

Experiments span several regimes of practical interest: a toy N-body system, a data-scarce/OOD ammonia benchmark with direct comparison to published baselines (Tan et al., 2023), fine-tuning a pretrained universal potential (ORB v3) on silica glass, and an active learning loop on MATPES.

The equivariance analysis is a valuable and honest contribution: the appendix clearly explains why the local reparameterization trick breaks equivariance for irrep-based models (MACE, UMA), and Proposition 1 formalizes when stochastic maps remain equivariant.
Hyperparameters, datasets, metrics (with explicit formulas for ECE, CRPS, NLL), and a computational cost analysis are documented in detail across the appendix.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: BLIP is essentially adaptive variational dropout (Kingma et al., 2015) applied to MPNN weights, explicitly following the BARNN recipe of Coscia et al. (2025). The core contribution is an application/transfer to interatomic potentials rather than a new inference technique, and the paper does not sufficiently delineate what is new beyond domain adaptation.

Central claims are stronger than the evidence. The abstract/introduction claim BLIP 'matches or exceeds' Deep Ensembles, but in the equivariant N-body setting (the setting most relevant to MLIPs) Deep Ensembles clearly outperform on all three metrics (MSE 0.057 vs 0.060, NLL -16.22 vs -12.52, CRPS 0.020 vs 0.022). On silica, BLIP also slightly underperforms the ensemble on error-uncertainty correlation (0.602 vs 0.676).

The equivariance story contains an internal contradiction. Section 3.3 states BLIP 'can be used in conjunction with equivariant or invariant MLIPs without violating their symmetry properties', yet Appendix A.3 concedes that the local reparameterization trick actually used in practice breaks equivariance for irrep-based architectures, and the method excludes MACE and UMA in its current form. This substantially weakens the 'architecture-agnostic' and 'seamlessly integrates with equivariant models' claims for the most important modern MLIPs.

The Bayesian framing is questionable: the prior variance is tied to the learned weights θ² (Eq. 9), i.e., the 'prior' depends on the parameters being inferred, and the KL derivations in A.1 treat θ as fixed. This undermines the claim of 'principled' Bayesian inference; the method is arguably closer to regularized stochastic weight perturbation.

Baseline coverage is thin. No comparison against other scalable UQ methods for NNPs beyond MC Dropout and Deep Ensembles (e.g., Laplace approximations, SWAG, SNGP, or the Bayesian approaches reviewed in Thaler et al., 2023, which the paper cites as closely related but never empirically compares to). Deep Ensemble results also lack variance estimates (±NA in Table 1), suggesting a single run.

Sensitivity and reproducibility concerns: each experiment requires substantially different, hand-tuned regularization settings (λ ranges from 0.001 to 10, prior dropout p from 0.01 to 0.5, different coefficient clamping ranges), with the silica setup explicitly adjusted because pretrained weights are 'highly sensitive to even minimal perturbations'. This raises the question of whether gains reflect the method or extensive per-task tuning, and no code release is mentioned.

Inconsistency in the efficiency narrative: the paper claims 'minimal computational overhead', but Table 6 shows ~1.9× training FLOPs, and uncertainty estimates require 100 stochastic forward passes (sample mean); the truly zero-overhead mode (MAP) provides no uncertainty. The AL experiment gains (e.g., forces 103.85 vs 105.12 meV/Å) are modest and lack an ensemble-acquisition baseline.

Writing and presentation have notable sloppiness (e.g., 'data-scarce'/'memebers', 'finetuning', inconsistent ensemble variance reporting, AL step counts described as '5 AL steps' vs 25 epochs), which reduces confidence in the overall rigor.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely important and practical problem: scalable, well-calibrated uncertainty quantification for MLIPs without the cost of deep ensembles, which is highly relevant to active learning and error-aware simulation workflows.

The method is architecture-agnostic within its scope and integrates cleanly with existing (equivariant) MPNNs; the equivariance analysis (Proposition 1 and Corollary 1, plus the discussion of why local reparameterization breaks equivariance for irreps) is a nice, honest technical contribution.

Experiments span a meaningful range of settings: a controlled N-body benchmark, a data-scarce/OOD regime (ammonia, following the protocol of Tan et al. 2023), fine-tuning a state-of-the-art pretrained model (ORB v3) on SiO2 at multiple data sizes, and a large-scale active learning experiment on MATPES. This is more comprehensive than typical UQ-for-MLIP evaluations.

The results support the central claims: BLIP matches or approaches deep ensembles on accuracy and calibration at a fraction of the cost, achieves the best ECE on the ammonia OOD benchmark, and demonstrates a clear benefit for uncertainty-guided active learning (Table 4, Figure 4).
The computational cost analysis (Appendix E, Table 6) is concrete and quantifies the claimed efficiency advantage over ensembles (~2x training FLOPs, 1x inference FLOPs vs NxN for ensembles).

Reproducibility is aided by public datasets, detailed hyperparameter tables (Table 5), pseudocode for training/inference, and explicit follow-through of prior work's protocols (e.g., Tan et al. 2023) for fair comparison.
Limitations are discussed candidly, notably the exclusion of irrep-based architectures (MACE, UMA) and the slightly worse Spearman correlation vs. deep ensembles in the SiO2 experiment.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is limited: the core technique is adaptive variational dropout (Kingma et al., 2015) with input-dependent coefficients, explicitly following Coscia et al. (2025) (BARNN), applied to MPNNs/MLIPs. The contribution is primarily a domain transfer plus engineering, which may fall short of the main track's originality bar.

A key empirical claim - that the *adaptive*, input-dependent coefficients are what matter - is not validated by ablation. There is no comparison against non-adaptive variational dropout (fixed alpha/beta), no sensitivity analysis of the KL weight lambda, inference network size, or clamping ranges, even though the appendix reveals highly dataset-specific tuning (lambda = 0.01 vs 10 vs 0.001; clamp ranges differing by orders of magnitude). It is plausible that the gains come from weight noise acting as regularizer rather than from principled Bayesian inference.

There is a tension between the claimed generality and the practical method: the efficient local-reparameterization implementation breaks equivariance for irrep-based networks, excluding MACE and UMA - arguably the most widely used modern equivariant MLIPs. The weight-sampling version is equivariant in principle (Corollary 1) but is not the version actually used, and its cost is not evaluated.

The prior variance is defined in terms of the learned mean weights (Eq. 9), making the prior input/parameter-dependent and the KL term (Eq. 10) not a divergence to a fixed prior; this well-known issue with variational dropout parameterizations is not discussed or analyzed.

Some comparisons are weakened by design: Deep Ensembles use only 4 members (with '±NA' entries suggesting single runs for some N-body baselines), and several ammonia/silica baselines are transcribed from Tan et al. (2023) rather than re-run. In the active learning experiment, the 'w/o BLIP' control is not fully specified (e.g., whether it also uses random pool selection), so the relative contributions of BLIP vs. the AL procedure are partially confounded.

Equivariance of individual stochastic forward passes is broken ('equivariant in distribution' only, per footnote 3); the consequences for force predictions in conservative models (per-sample -∇E of non-equivariant sampled energies) and for downstream MD stability are not examined.
No code release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility of a method whose performance appears sensitive to clamping and lambda choices.

Presentation has noticeable issues: typos ('data-scarse', 'memebers', 'finetuing', 'the once induced'), and the N-body GNN results show BLIP slightly behind Deep Ensemble in the equivariant setting, which the text somewhat glosses over.
